title: DAVID TOOK MORE WIVES AND CONCUBINES AFTER GOD MADE HIM KING—BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS NEXT
paragraphs: DAVID TOOK MORE WIVES AND CONCUBINES AFTER GOD MADE HIM KING—BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT THE BIBLE SAYS NEXT

He was chosen by God, anointed as king, and remembered as a man after God's own heart. Yet behind the palace walls, David was building a household that contradicted God's design. And the consequences would reach far beyond his own bedroom. This is the uncomfortable truth about power, compromise, grace, and why even the greatest earthly king desperately needed Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about reading the Bible carefully.
Not because Scripture is confused.
But because sometimes it tells us things about people we admire that we would rather not know.
We love David standing before Goliath.
We love David worshiping with all his might.
We love David writing psalms through tears, trusting God in caves, and refusing to kill Saul when he had the opportunity.
We love the shepherd boy who became king.
But what happens when that same David becomes powerful enough to take more wives and concubines?
What happens when the man who once depended on God for everything begins accumulating things God never intended a king to accumulate?
And what happens when the Bible records it without immediately interrupting the story to condemn him?
That is where many readers make a dangerous mistake.
They assume that because God allowed something to happen, God must have approved of it.
But there is a difference between what Scripture records and what Scripture commands.
And if we fail to understand that difference, we can turn the failures of biblical heroes into permission slips for our own disobedience.
Listen carefully to what the Bible actually says.
“And David took him more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem, after he was come from Hebron: and there were yet sons and daughters born to David.” — 2 Samuel 5:13, King James Version
Read that again.
Not before David became king.
Not while he was running for his life.
Not while hiding in a wilderness cave.
After he came from Hebron to Jerusalem.
After his kingship had been established over all Israel.
After God had opened doors that no human being could have opened for him.
And just two verses earlier, Scripture had said something remarkable:
“And David went on, and grew great, and the LORD God of hosts was with him.” — 2 Samuel 5:10, KJV
Now place those two statements beside each other.
The Lord was with David.
And David took more wives and concubines.
The first statement describes God's gracious presence in establishing David's kingship.
The second records a royal practice that stood in tension with God's instructions for Israel's kings.
One does not automatically justify the other.
And that distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because a person can experience genuine blessings from God while still carrying areas of serious disobedience.
A ministry can grow while its leader needs correction.
A family can prosper while hidden wounds remain unaddressed.
A person can know Scripture, pray sincerely, serve faithfully, and still have habits that need to be surrendered.
God's faithfulness must never be mistaken for His approval of everything we do.
And perhaps that is why this passage is so uncomfortable.
Because David's story is not merely about a king who lived thousands of years ago.
It raises a question about every human heart.
What do we do with the blessings God places in our hands?
Do they make us more dependent on Him?
Or do they slowly convince us that we no longer need to listen as carefully?
The original Hebrew makes the verse especially worth examining.
The opening words of 2 Samuel 5:13 are:
וַיִּקַּח דָּוִד עוֹד פִּלַגְשִׁים וְנָשִׁים
Transliterated:
Vayyiqqaḥ David ʿod pilagshim venashim.
A careful rendering is:
“And David took more concubines and wives.”
The Hebrew verb וַיִּקַּח (vayyiqqaḥ) comes from לָקַח (laqach), meaning “to take.” In this context, it describes David acquiring additional women as part of his royal household.
The word עוֹד (ʿod) carries the sense of “more” or “additional.”
And the two nouns are significant.
פִּלַגְשִׁים (pilagshim) means “concubines.”
נָשִׁים (nashim) means “women” or, in this context, “wives.”

A concubine in the ancient Near Eastern world was generally a woman in a recognized but lower-status union than that of a principal wife. Her position and legal protections could differ from those of a wife, and her relationship to the household was shaped by the patriarchal structures of that society.
The text does not tell us how each woman entered David's household, whether every relationship involved willing consent, or how these women personally experienced their circumstances.
We must not invent details Scripture does not give.
But we should not overlook what it does reveal.
David was expanding his royal household.
And the wording makes clear that these women were additional to those he already had.
This was not simply a man getting married for the first time.
This was a king accumulating more wives and concubines after becoming established in Jerusalem.
In the ancient world, royal marriages could serve political, dynastic, and diplomatic purposes. Large royal households could also communicate status and power.
But historical custom is not the same as divine permission.
And this is where the story becomes even more revealing.
Long before David sat on a throne, God had already spoken about the conduct of Israel's future kings.
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.” — Deuteronomy 17:17, KJV
The Hebrew phrase is:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
Velo yarbeh-lo nashim.
“And he shall not multiply wives for himself.”
Notice the concern.
God was not merely regulating royal appearances.
He was guarding the king's heart.
The warning continues:
“That his heart turn not away.”
The issue was not simply how many people lived in the palace.
It was whether the king's desires, alliances, and loyalties would pull his heart away from the Lord.
David had been entrusted with authority.
But authority did not place him above God's Word.
The king was supposed to live under the covenant, not above it.

In fact, Deuteronomy 17:18–20 required Israel's king to have a copy of God's law, read it throughout his life, fear the Lord, obey His commandments, and refuse to exalt his heart above his fellow Israelites.
Imagine that.
The man sitting on Israel's throne was supposed to remain a student of God's Word.
Not its exception.
Not its editor.
Not someone who could quietly change the rules because he had become successful.
And suddenly, 2 Samuel 5:13 becomes more than an ancient record of royal marriages.
It becomes a warning about the spiritual danger of increasing power without increasing obedience.
Because sometimes the greatest test of faith does not arrive when everything is falling apart.
Sometimes it arrives when everything seems to be going well.
When the money starts coming.
When the recognition increases.
When people begin respecting your name.
When opportunities open.
When nobody questions your decisions anymore.
When you have enough influence to make your desires look reasonable.
That is when a person must be especially careful.
Not because success is inherently sinful.
But because success can expose desires that hardship once restrained.
David knew what it meant to have nothing.
He knew what it meant to be hunted, rejected, betrayed, and misunderstood.
He had cried out to God from places where human strength could not save him.
Yet being delivered from danger did not mean he was delivered from every temptation.
And the same is true of us.
You can survive a season of suffering and still stumble in a season of comfort.
You can endure persecution and still be weakened by praise.
You can resist temptation when you have no opportunity to act on it, only to discover how powerful that temptation becomes when the opportunity finally arrives.
That is why spiritual maturity cannot be measured merely by what we have survived.
It must also be seen in how we obey when we have choices.
And there is another painful reality hidden beneath this passage.
David's wives and concubines were not merely symbols of royal wealth.
They were human beings.
Women with lives, emotions, relationships, and personal histories.
Their children would grow up within a complicated royal household.
Some of those children would eventually become central figures in deeply tragic events.
Scripture does not say that every later tragedy in David's family resulted directly from the marriages recorded in 2 Samuel 5:13.
We should not force a simple explanation onto a complicated biblical narrative.
But the books of Samuel do reveal a household marked by rivalry, abuse, grief, rebellion, and bloodshed.
Amnon would sexually assault his half-sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13).
Absalom would later arrange Amnon's death (2 Samuel 13).
Absalom would rebel against David and publicly take his father's concubines as part of his attempt to seize the kingdom (2 Samuel 16:21–22).
And David would eventually mourn the death of Absalom with a father's devastating cry:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” — 2 Samuel 18:33, KJV
The same palace that represented David's royal achievement would become the setting of terrible family suffering.
And before anyone uses this story to shame a wounded family, we need to remember something important.
The Bible does not teach that every broken family is the result of one parent's particular sin.
Nor does it place responsibility for violence upon its victims.
Amnon was responsible for what he did to Tamar.
Absalom was responsible for his own actions.
David was responsible for his.
Every person must be treated with moral seriousness.
But Scripture also refuses to pretend that our choices exist in isolation.
What we tolerate can affect people who never agreed to carry the consequences.
A father's compromise can wound a household.
A leader's misconduct can damage a community.
A private sin can eventually become a public sorrow.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
Maybe you grew up in a home where everyone looked respectable outside, but inside there were secrets nobody was allowed to discuss.
Maybe you watched a parent preach values they did not practice.
Maybe you have been hurt by someone who used spiritual language to excuse behavior that contradicted Scripture.
Maybe you have even been the person who made those compromises.
You still believe in God.
You still love Jesus.
But there is something in your life that you keep trying to explain away.
Something you know needs to change.
And the most dangerous sentence you keep telling yourself is:
“God is still blessing me, so maybe it isn't that serious.”
But David's story will not allow us to confuse God's patience with moral approval.
Nor should we confuse God's mercy with the absence of consequences.
And if we follow David's story further, the warning becomes even more serious.
Years after the events of 2 Samuel 5, David would see Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, bathing.
He would send for her.
He would sleep with her.
And after she became pregnant, David would attempt to conceal what had happened.
When his efforts failed, he arranged circumstances that led to Uriah's death in battle.
You can read the account in 2 Samuel 11.
It is a disturbing story involving a king's power, sexual wrongdoing, deception, and the killing of an innocent man.
We should not romanticize it.
Nor should we treat Bathsheba as though the text establishes that she shared equal power or responsibility with the king who summoned her.
The narrative places decisive responsibility upon David.
And then comes one of the most frightening sentences in the account.
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 11:27, KJV
David may have concealed his actions from much of the kingdom.
But he had not concealed them from God.
The palace could not hide him.
His crown could not protect him from divine judgment.
His reputation could not rewrite what had happened.
And the God who had lifted him from the sheepfold would not call evil good simply because David was His chosen king.
Then God sent Nathan.
The prophet confronted David through a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only beloved lamb.
David became furious at the injustice.
He could see another man's wrongdoing clearly.
Until Nathan spoke the words that shattered his self-protection.
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7, KJV
Four words.
No flattering introduction.
No attempt to protect the king's image.
No assurance that his achievements somehow canceled his sin.
Just truth.
Thou art the man.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being about David and begins confronting us.
Because it is possible to recognize sin in someone else while remaining blind to the same kind of darkness in ourselves.
We can condemn dishonesty while hiding our own.
We can criticize unfaithfulness while entertaining temptation.
We can demand accountability from leaders while refusing accountability in our homes.
We can quote Scripture to correct others while avoiding the passages that correct us.
And sometimes the most loving thing God can do is allow His Word to expose the excuses we have carefully built around our disobedience.
Not to destroy us.
But to bring us into the light.
David's response matters.
“And David said unto Nathan, I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
No long defense is recorded in that moment.
No appeal to his royal position.
No attempt to blame Uriah.
No claim that kings simply lived differently.
He acknowledged his sin.
That confession did not erase the damage.
It did not bring Uriah back to life.
It did not undo Bathsheba's suffering.
It did not remove every painful consequence that followed.
But it marked the beginning of an honest return to God.
And Psalm 51 gives us a profound window into the language of David's repentance.
Its superscription connects the psalm to Nathan's confrontation with David concerning Bathsheba.
David prayed:
“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.” — Psalm 51:1, KJV
The Hebrew begins:
חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ
Chonneni Elohim kechasdecha.
“Be gracious to me, O God, according to Your steadfast love.”
The word חֶסֶד (chesed) speaks of steadfast love, covenant loyalty, and enduring kindness.
David was not asking God to pretend he had done nothing wrong.
He was appealing to God's mercy because he knew he had done wrong.
And later he prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from the Hebrew root ברא (bara), meaning “to create.”
David did not merely ask for a better public image.
He asked God to create a clean heart within him.
He understood that his deepest problem could not be solved by polishing the outside.
He needed inner renewal.
And that is still our need.
Not simply better religious appearances.
Not merely a more carefully managed reputation.
Not another promise that we will try harder while secretly protecting the same sin.
We need God's transforming grace.
We need forgiveness.
We need a new heart.
We need a Savior.
And this is where David's story becomes far greater than David himself.
Because if we stop at the lesson that powerful people should resist temptation, we have not yet reached the heart of the Gospel.
David was a remarkable king in many ways.
But he was not the perfect king.
He could defeat Goliath.
But he could not defeat sin through his own strength.
He could lead armies.
But he could not rule his own desires perfectly.
He could write songs of worship.
But he could not make himself righteous before God.
And despite everything God accomplished through him, David was never meant to be humanity's final hope.
Someone greater had to come.
Someone who would possess authority without abusing it.
Someone who would face temptation without surrendering to it.
Someone who would love without exploiting.
Someone who would reign without corruption.
Someone whose obedience would not collapse under the weight of power.
And that Someone is Jesus Christ.
The New Testament introduces Jesus as the promised Son of David.
“The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.” — Matthew 1:1, KJV
In Greek, the opening identifies Him as:
Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ υἱοῦ Δαυὶδ
Iēsou Christou huiou Dauid.
“Jesus Christ, son of David.”
The title huiou Dauid connects Jesus to the royal promises associated with David's house.
God had promised David that his kingdom would have an enduring future (2 Samuel 7:12–16).
The New Testament presents Jesus as the fulfillment of that royal hope.
But Jesus did not come merely to repeat David's kingship.
He came to fulfill what David's kingship could never accomplish.
David was anointed, but he sinned.
Jesus is the Christ—the Anointed One—and He remained without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
David sometimes used royal power for himself.
Jesus declared:
“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Mark 10:45, KJV
David took what did not belong to him.
Jesus willingly gave His own life to save sinners.
David's actions brought suffering upon others.
Jesus willingly bore suffering to accomplish redemption.
David needed forgiveness.
Jesus came to provide it.
And here is the extraordinary beauty of the Gospel.
God did not erase David's failures from Scripture in order to protect the reputation of the royal family through which the Messiah would come.
The Bible tells the truth.
Even when that truth is painful.
Even when it exposes the failures of its most celebrated figures.
Even when it reminds us that the family history of the Messiah includes human sin, sorrow, and scandal.
Matthew 1:6 refers to Solomon's mother as the woman who had been Uriah's wife.
That wording keeps the memory of David's wrongdoing within the genealogy itself.
The Gospel does not require us to pretend the scandal never happened.
It reveals the Savior who came into a world full of scandals to redeem sinners.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
Not because the wounded should simply forget what happened.
But because Jesus Christ entered the broken history of humanity to accomplish what no fallen king could do.
He came to save.
He came to reconcile.
He came to make forgiveness possible through His death and resurrection.
He came to call sinners to repentance and new life.
And He came to establish a kingdom that cannot be corrupted by the failures of an earthly ruler.
This does not mean that grace erases every earthly consequence.
David was forgiven, yet he still faced profound sorrow.
A person who has harmed others may receive God's forgiveness while remaining responsible for confession, restitution where possible, changed behavior, and appropriate accountability.
Forgiveness is not permission to continue abusing power.
Repentance is not a performance designed to silence the wounded.
And grace is never an excuse to return comfortably to the sin from which Christ calls us.
The apostle Paul asked:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The Greek response begins:
μὴ γένοιτο
Mē genoito.
An emphatic rejection, often rendered:
“By no means!”
Grace does not teach us to make peace with sin.
Grace calls us out of its dominion.
That is why the Gospel is both deeply comforting and deeply confronting.
It comforts the sinner who fears they are beyond forgiveness.
And it confronts the sinner who wants forgiveness without surrender.
It welcomes the broken.
And it refuses to call the chains holding them captive a blessing.
Perhaps you have reached this point in the article carrying a burden nobody else knows about.
Maybe you have spent years hiding behind your usefulness to others.
You provide for your family.
You help at church.
You encourage people online.
You speak about faith.
But in private, there is a battle you keep losing.
Maybe it is lust.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe it is a relationship you know is drawing you away from obedience.
Maybe it is bitterness you have nourished for years.
Maybe it is dishonesty, selfish ambition, or the quiet belief that your position makes you an exception.
Or perhaps you are not the one who caused the harm.
Perhaps you are the one still carrying it.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone misused your trust.
Someone told you to remain silent for the sake of a family, a ministry, or a reputation.
And the story of David has made you wonder whether God truly sees what powerful people do.
He does.
The same Scriptures that record David's achievements also expose his sins.
God did not need to protect David's image by hiding the truth.
And you do not need to deny your pain in order to honor God.
The Lord cares about righteousness and truth.
He is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).
And His invitation to come to Him is not limited to those whose lives appear respectable.
Jesus said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
That invitation is not a command to pretend.
It is an invitation to come.
With the shame.
With the questions.
With the wounds.
With the guilt that needs repentance.
With the grief that needs comfort.
With the habits that need to be surrendered.
With the memories that still make your chest tighten when the room becomes quiet.
Come to Christ.
Not because your story is already clean.
But because He is the Savior of sinners.
And if you have wandered far from God, remember what the apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
The promise does not depend on your ability to manufacture a perfect past.
It rests upon God's faithfulness and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Yet that promise also calls us into the light.
Confession means we stop defending what God calls sin.
Repentance means we turn toward Him.
Faith means we entrust ourselves to Christ rather than our own righteousness.
And transformation means we begin learning to live under His lordship.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without struggle.
But no longer treating sin as a permanent home.
And if David's story teaches us anything about spiritual danger, it is that we must never wait until the consequences become catastrophic before taking God's warnings seriously.
A small compromise deserves attention before it becomes a destructive pattern.
An unhealthy desire deserves surrender before it becomes an act of betrayal.
A secret habit deserves honest confrontation before it begins controlling the heart.
The question is not simply whether God has blessed you.
The question is whether you are listening to Him.
Whether you are willing to let His Word correct you.
Whether you will surrender even the things that have become comfortable.
Because Jesus did not die merely to improve our image.
He died and rose again to reconcile us to God and give us new life.
And there is no earthly crown worth losing your soul over.
No pleasure worth hardening your heart against Christ.
No secret worth protecting at the expense of truth.
No public reputation worth preserving through continued wrongdoing.
David's story is a warning.
But it is also a testimony that the last word does not have to belong to sin.
God's mercy is real.
His holiness is real.
His forgiveness is real.
And His power to transform lives is real.
If this article has exposed something you have been avoiding, you do not need to disclose private details publicly. But I invite you to respond with a simple, sincere prayer.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and their past does not have to determine their future.
And if this truth brought someone to your mind, do not let that thought disappear.
Maybe it is a friend who has drifted away from church.
A brother who is struggling in secret.
A sister who has been wounded by betrayal.
A parent who needs encouragement.
A young believer who admires David but has never been taught how to read the difficult parts of his story.
Not merely to increase its reach, but to place Scripture where someone who would never search for a sermon might encounter it.

And if you believe that Scripture-centered teaching like this should continue reaching families, struggling believers, seekers, and people who have almost given up on faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
Not to glorify a personality.
Not to excuse sin.
Not to build a following around controversy.
But to proclaim the Gospel, teach the Word of God, encourage repentance, strengthen discipleship, and remind broken people that the grace of Christ is greater than the darkness of their past.
It can help sustain the creation of Scripture-centered articles, discipleship materials, encouragement, and outreach to more readers.
The New Testament teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Giving that honors God is not forced by fear or guilt.
It comes from a willing heart.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to encourage conversations about faith.
But voluntary support from those who are able can help the work continue.
But before you leave, return with me to Jerusalem.
To David.
To that single verse.
“And David took him more concubines and wives...”
At first glance, it looks like an ordinary record of ancient royal life.
But when we read it beside God's command in Deuteronomy, and then follow the larger story of David's life, we begin to understand the danger of allowing success to silence obedience.
David was a great king.
But greatness did not make him sinless.
David was loved by God.
But that love did not make his wrongdoing righteous.
David was forgiven.
But forgiveness did not mean his actions were harmless.
And David was part of God's redemptive plan.
But David was not the Redeemer.
Jesus is.
That is the truth we must carry away from this story.
Do not build your faith on the perfection of biblical heroes.
Build it on the perfection of Jesus Christ.
Do not use another person's failure to justify your own.
Allow God's Word to search your heart.
Do not mistake prosperity for proof that everything in your life pleases God.
Measure your life by His truth.
And do not believe that your worst failure automatically places you beyond the reach of His mercy.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
He is not merely a better version of David.
He is the promised King, the crucified and risen Savior, the righteous Lord whose kingdom will never end.
David's crown could not save him from sin.
But the Son of David wore a crown of thorns to save sinners like us.
And that is why the Gospel is not a story about human beings becoming impressive enough for God to love them.
It is the story of the holy God who loved sinners and sent His Son to redeem them.
So when you look at your past, do not pretend it never happened.
When you face your sin, do not defend it.
When you see your wounds, do not assume God has forgotten you.
Bring everything into the light of Christ.
Let His truth confront what needs repentance.
Let His grace comfort what needs healing.
Let His Word reshape what needs changing.
And let His love teach you to walk in obedience.
Because the greatest miracle in David's story was never that a shepherd became a king.
It was that God's redemptive promise continued through a deeply flawed man and ultimately led to the only King who could save us.
David needed a Savior even after he wore the crown. And so do we, no matter how successful, respected, religious, or strong we appear.
